clinicalPearls: A benign inherited cause of lifelong mild hypercalcaemia that mimics primary hyperparathyroidism
It is usually asymptomatic and detected incidentally on biochemistry
Parathyroid hormone is normal or mildly elevated, similar to primary hyperparathyroidism, but urinary calcium excretion is characteristically low
The calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio is typically low and helps distinguish it from primary hyperparathyroidism
Most cases are due to inactivating mutations of the calcium-sensing receptor gene (CASR), inherited in an autosomal dominant manner
Recognising it prevents unnecessary parathyroid surgery, which does not correct the hypercalcaemia
reference.pathophysiology: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia most often results from a heterozygous inactivating mutation of the calcium-sensing receptor. This receptor, expressed in the parathyroid glands and renal tubules, normally senses extracellular calcium and suppresses parathyroid hormone secretion and promotes renal calcium excretion as calcium rises. With reduced receptor sensitivity, the set-point for calcium is reset upward, so mild hypercalcaemia persists with inappropriately normal parathyroid hormone, and the kidney avidly reabsorbs calcium, producing the characteristic hypocalciuria.
additionalInvestigations: Twenty-four-hour urinary calcium and calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio
Family history and, where available, CASR genetic testing
redFlags: Features suggesting an alternative cause such as malignancy
Marked or symptomatic hypercalcaemia atypical for the condition
Neonatal severe hyperparathyroidism in homozygous CASR disease
Renal calculi or end-organ effects suggesting another diagnosis
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign with an excellent prognosis and generally requires no treatment, only recognition and avoidance of inappropriate parathyroid surgery.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for primary hyperparathyroidism and performing parathyroidectomy
Not measuring urinary calcium before considering surgery
Overlooking a family history of asymptomatic hypercalcaemia
Confounding urine calcium by concurrent thiazide use or vitamin D deficiency
management: Recognise the condition as benign and avoid parathyroidectomy, which does not correct the calcium-sensing receptor defect
Provide reassurance, as the typical heterozygous form requires no specific pharmacological therapy
Confirm the diagnosis biochemically with a low calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio before treating apparent primary hyperparathyroidism
Maintain adequate hydration and avoid aggravating factors such as thiazide diuretics, lithium and excess vitamin D or calcium supplementation
Reserve a calcimimetic (cinacalcet) for the rare genuinely symptomatic patient
Undertake family biochemical screening and genetic counselling for autosomal dominant CASR inheritance
Escalate urgently if a neonate born to two carrier parents presents with severe hypercalcaemia (neonatal severe hyperparathyroidism), which may require urgent parathyroidectomy
